kurz: Eight mental models from physics, biology, engineering and economics, and what each of them reveals about a German portfolio.

bloecke.md:
Charlie Munger never described his method as an investment strategy. He saw it as compensation for a gap in education. Anyone who masters only one school of thought applies its patterns to every situation. Munger compares this to a man who has only a hammer and sees a nail in every problem. He calls his antidote a [[Latticework|latticework]], a grid of a few important models from different disciplines. New experiences can be slotted into it and so stay in the memory instead of being lost as isolated anecdotes.

Eight of these models are particularly useful in money matters. Each is explained here using a verifiable figure rather than a metaphor. The last section deals with the more important question of what applies when two of them contradict each other.

## Economies of scale

An index fund has mainly fixed costs. The index licence, custodian bank, audit and regulatory reporting cost roughly the same whether the fund manages €200 million or €20 billion. With every additional euro, the same costs are spread over a larger asset base. That is why the largest world ETFs have the lowest ongoing charges. A low expense ratio is therefore a consequence of volume and not evidence of skill.

Beyond a certain size, however, economies of scale turn into diseconomies of scale. An active fund that moves double-digit billions can no longer buy small caps without its own orders shifting the price to its disadvantage. Buffett and Munger have written about their own company that the percentage gains of the first fifty years cannot be repeated because the base has become too large.

In the Morningstar Active/Passive Barometer (as of June 2025), 27% of the cheapest active funds did better over ten years than their passive counterpart, but only 15% of the most expensive ones. In the US Large Blend category, the figures were 15.4% and 3.9%. Costs are the only factor there that consistently predicts success.

## Incentive systems

At the top of Munger's list of cognitive biases is the reward and punishment superresponse tendency. People reliably do what they are paid for and in the process regard it as their own conviction. When it comes to advice, it therefore helps little to ask what someone recommends. The useful question is how that person is paid and what happens to them if the advice turns out badly.

In Germany, the incentive depends on the distribution channel. For investment services, inducements from third parties are permitted under Section 70 WpHG (Securities Trading Act) only if they improve the quality of the service, and they must be disclosed. Fee-based investment advice (Honorar-Anlageberatung) under Section 64(5) WpHG may only be paid by the client and must pass on to the client any inducements that cannot be avoided. For unit-linked life and pension insurance, the acquisition and distribution costs are spread over the first five years for calculation purposes under Section 169(3) VVG (Insurance Contract Act). That is why a policy surrendered in the third year is worth less than the sum of the premiums.

A bet that Buffett entered into in 2007 and settled in 2017 shows how expensive an incentive can become over ten years. In it, a simple S&P 500 index fund competed against five funds of hedge funds, which together held more than 200 underlying funds. Buffett attributed the result to the fees and not to a lack of skill on the part of the managers. The funds of funds charged fixed fees of around 2.5% on the amount invested, regardless of the result.

bloecke.md:
## Redundancy

Engineers design load-bearing structures for a multiple of the expected load. They also build in second systems that only start working when the first one fails. Graham's margin of safety transfers this principle to investing. He only bought net-nets when they cost less than two thirds of their net current assets. A miscalculation or bad luck therefore did not immediately lead to a permanent loss of capital.

In a household, redundancy includes an emergency fund outside the portfolio, a second means of access to money through a second bank, financing that remains affordable even at a significantly higher follow-up interest rate, and protection for your ability to work instead of relying on your income continuing until 67. This provision costs return in ninety-nine years out of a hundred. In the hundredth year, it ensures that you are not forced to sell.

## Critical mass

The term comes from nuclear physics. Below a threshold nothing happens; above it, the reaction runs by itself. In money matters there are three such thresholds. The first is fund size. Funds that remain too small are closed or merged. In Europe, only 58% of equity funds and 54% of bond funds survived over ten years, and in the first half of 2025 alone, 2.4% disappeared. The second is order size. With a fixed fee of €4.90, a €25 order costs 19.6% of the amount invested, a €500 order 0.98%. The third is the portfolio size at which tax becomes due on the ongoing income in the first place.

The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) is €1,000 per person, or €2,000 for joint assessment (Section 20(9) EStG, Income Tax Act). For equity funds, there is also the [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)]] of 30% for assets held privately (Section 20(1) InvStG, Investment Tax Act). So only 70% of the income is taxable. Illustrative calculation with annual income of 2% before partial exemption, as a distribution or as the advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale) under Section 18 InvStG:

`€1,000 ÷ (0.02 × 0.70) ≈ €71,400`

Up to a portfolio value of around €71,000, the income stays within the allowance. Below this limit, no tax is due on the ongoing income. Tax planning can then only make use of the unused remainder of the allowance, for example to realise price gains tax-free by selling and buying back.

## Feedback loops

Cybernetics distinguishes between damping feedback, which steers a system back, and reinforcing feedback, which amplifies every deviation. Both operate in the market, but the reinforcing kind is more noticeable. Rising prices generate attention, attention generates inflows and inflows generate rising prices, until the loop changes sign.

Morningstar's 2026 study “Mind the Gap” gives an indication of what the loop costs investors. According to it, the investor return in the decade to 31 December 2025 was 8.7% a year, while the funds themselves achieved 9.9%. The difference of 1.2 points arises solely from the timing and size of purchases and sales. Not all of the difference is due to the loop, however, because a gap also arises without any behavioural mistakes if the amount invested grows through regular contributions and the later years turn out weaker than the earlier ones. The gap grows with the fluctuation of the product. It is around 0.4 points in the calmest fifth of funds and over 2 points in the most volatile fifth, around 2.5 points for international equity ETFs and zero for US large blend funds.

bloecke.md:
## Entropy

Without an input of energy, systems pass into the more probable, more disordered state. A portfolio is no exception. Its allocation drifts, and over time old contracts, second securities accounts and individual positions from special situations accumulate. The drift can be calculated. In a 60/40 portfolio whose equity portion grows at 8% and whose bond portion grows at 2% a year, the equity allocation after ten years without a single intervention is around 73%. The portfolio thus has a different risk profile without anyone having decided so.

bloecke.titel: Shift from 60/40 to almost 73/27 in ten years without rebalancing
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with 8% growth in the equity portion and 2% in the bond portion, without contributions. The risk rises because nobody resets the allocation.

bloecke.md: Correcting the drift through sales triggers a tax payment. When units of the same kind are sold, the order of acquisition applies (Section 20(4) sentence 7 EStG). The realised gain is subject to 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) plus solidarity surcharge (Section 32d(1) EStG), 26.375% in total. For equity funds, the partial exemption reduces the burden to an effective 18.46% of the gain. Small deviations are therefore corrected through new contributions, and only large ones through sales. Directing new money into the underweight portion is cheaper than restructuring the existing portfolio.

## Opportunity cost

In economics, nothing has a price on its own. The price of a decision is the best alternative you give up for it. Munger turned this into a test rule. According to it, an opportunity only comes into question if it is better than the best one already available. Being good in itself is not enough.

The measurement method of the Morningstar barometer also follows this model. It compares active funds with the cost-adjusted average of the index funds in the same category, that is, with an alternative that investors can buy. An index that nobody can buy does not serve as the yardstick. Only 21% of active US strategies survived the ten years to June 2025 while beating their passive counterpart; in the period to June 2026, the figure was around 25%. For European equity funds, the proportion over ten years was 11.9%.

bloecke.formel: Advantage = return of the choice after costs and taxes − return of the best available alternative after costs and taxes
bloecke.erklaerung: Both sides of the comparison must be on the same footing, that is, after costs, after taxes and with the same certainty. If you set an expected return against a certain interest rate, you are comparing two different things. The difference is then a risk premium and does not indicate superiority.
bloecke.beispiel: Special repayment at an assumed borrowing rate of 3.9% versus an equity fund with an assumed gross return of 7%: 7% × (1 − 0.1846) ≈ 5.7% net. The difference of around 1.8 points compensates for the fact that the fund's result can fluctuate, while the saving from the special repayment is certain.

bloecke.md:
## Selection

In biology, the sample is always biased, because whatever did not survive is also missing from museum collections. It is the same with fund rankings. Of the active US equity funds that existed twenty years ago, only 37.3% were still around at the end of the period. Over fifteen years the figure was 50.9%, over ten years 63.8%. The rest were closed or merged and are missing from every statistic that looks only at today's funds. The SPIVA scorecards therefore include the funds that have disappeared. Over twenty years, they arrive at a proportion of 93.8% that did worse than the benchmark index. The same [[Survivorship bias|survivorship bias]] affects people. Of a thousand who start a strategy, it is those for whom it worked out who write about it.

bloecke.titel: Survival rate of active funds to the end of the period
bloecke.unter: SPIVA U.S. and SPIVA Europe, Mid-Year 2025. Rankings that compare only today's funds leave out the missing part entirely, and this part is not randomly composed.

bloecke.md:
## Limits of a single model

The models partly contradict each other, and that is precisely what makes them useful. According to the model of economies of scale, bigger is cheaper; according to the same economics, bigger is more cumbersome in active management. Redundancy requires reserves; opportunity cost shows that reserves earn nothing. Critical mass argues against the small fund; selection explains why it looks so good today. With only one model, you get an unambiguous answer every time. You get it wrong in the cases in which a second model would have contradicted it.

Munger's [[Lollapalooza effect]] describes the opposite case, in which several forces act in the same direction at the same time. Social proof, envy, authority and the urge to act then drive the same purchase. The effects reinforce each other to an extreme instead of evening out to an average. This cannot be recognised with a single model, because each force can be explained on its own.

Mental models provide questions, but no ready-made answers. Where they confirm each other, they add little. They become useful where two of them point in different directions, because that is where the decision begins.

Every result can be explained afterwards with some model or other, rising prices with economies of scale, for example, and falling ones with entropy. Such explanations are stories and not analysis. A model is only of use if it makes a statement in advance that could be wrong, for example which figure you expect and at what value you would change your mind.

- For the incentive, clarify who earns from your commitment and how much.
- Compare the alternative after costs, after taxes and at the same level of certainty.
- For the threshold, check whether you and the product exceed the critical size.
- For feedback, check whether the step reinforces a movement that is already under way.
- For redundancy, clarify what remains if the assumption on which everything depends is wrong.
- For selection, ask about the cases that did not survive and are therefore missing.

Munger set out his method in 1994 in a talk at the USC Marshall School of Business (“A Lesson on Elementary, Worldly Wisdom”) and added his 25 cognitive biases in “The Psychology of Human Misjudgment”. Both texts are included in “Poor Charlie's Almanack”. The selection of models is not fixed. Further models, for example from statistics, law or behavioural biology, make the grid denser without distorting it.

mitnehmen: A single mental model always delivers an unambiguous answer and is dangerous for that very reason, because it does not reveal contradictions.
The four models with the greatest effect on a German portfolio are incentives, costs and scale, opportunity cost after taxes, and selection in statistics.
The entropy of a portfolio can be calculated, because without rebalancing a 60/40 portfolio turns arithmetically into one of around 73/27 in ten years.
Rebalancing through sales costs 26.375% tax on the gain, effectively 18.46% for equity funds, which is why new contributions are the cheaper route.
Where two models contradict each other lies the assumption that needs to be checked.

begriffe.text: Munger's image of a lattice of important mental models from different disciplines into which experiences can be fitted. It is the counter-model to the specialist who tackles every situation with the same tool.

Munger's term for several psychological tendencies acting together in the same direction. The result goes beyond the sum of the individual effects and leads to extremes such as bubbles, Ponzi schemes or panic selling.

Bias that arises because failures disappear from the sample. Fund rankings, for example, show only survivors, even though just under two thirds of active US equity funds were closed or merged over twenty years.
The price of a decision, measured against the best alternative that is actually available. Opportunity cost is only correctly calculated after costs, after taxes and at comparable certainty.

Flat-rate tax exemption for part of the income from investment funds under Section 20 InvStG. For equity funds held as private assets it is 30%, which reduces the effective burden from 26.375% to 18.46% of the gain.
